unit.title: Building a Government Study Tool
unit.subtitle: Who should have the power to decide? Learn the vocabulary, follow the delegates through Philadelphia, and see how the Constitution still shapes your life.
unit.essentialQuestion: Who should have the power to decide?

vocabulary.definition: The first written plan of government for the United States, in effect from 1781 to 1789
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: The country's first rulebook. It kept the states strong and the national government weak, with no president, no national courts and no power to tax.
vocabulary.example: Under the Articles of Confederation, Congress could only ask the states for money, and Rhode Island's no vote blocked a national tax in 1782.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: The Articles of Confederation were the first written plan of government for the United States. They created a weak national government with no president and no power to tax.

vocabulary.definition: A loose union of independent states that agree to work together for a common purpose
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: A team where every member keeps most of its own power and only agrees to cooperate on a few things.
vocabulary.example: The thirteen states formed a confederation in 1781, promising to defend one another but each keeping most of its own power.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A confederation is a loose union of independent states. Each state keeps most of its power and agrees to work with the others on a few shared goals.

vocabulary.definition: A 1787 law that set up a government for the land north of the Ohio River, explained how it could become new states, and banned slavery there
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: One of the few things Congress got right under the Articles: a plan for turning western land into new, equal states.
vocabulary.example: Because of the Northwest Ordinance, Ohio, Indiana and Illinois later joined the union as free states.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 explained how land north of the Ohio River could become new states. It also banned slavery in that region.

vocabulary.definition: A formal meeting held for a special purpose
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: A big, official meeting where people come together to make decisions about one important job.
vocabulary.example: In the summer of 1787, delegates from twelve states met at a convention in Philadelphia.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A convention is a formal meeting held for a special purpose. The meeting in Philadelphia in 1787 wrote the Constitution.

vocabulary.definition: A person chosen to represent others at a meeting
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Someone sent to speak and vote for a larger group that cannot all be in the room.
vocabulary.example: Virginia sent seven men to Philadelphia, including James Madison and George Washington, to speak for the state.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A delegate is a person chosen to represent others. Each state sent delegates to the meeting in Philadelphia.

vocabulary.definition: Being part of a group and having a voice in it
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Having a seat at the table when decisions are made.
vocabulary.example: In 1787, white men who owned property had a voice in choosing the new government.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: To be included means to be part of a group and have a voice in it. In 1787, only some Americans had that voice.

vocabulary.definition: Kept out of a group or left without a voice in it
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Shut out of the room where decisions are made, even when those decisions affect you.
vocabulary.example: Women, enslaved people and Native nations had no one at the meeting in Philadelphia.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: To be excluded means to be kept out. Women, enslaved people and Native nations had no voice at the meeting in Philadelphia.

vocabulary.definition: A country governed by representatives that the citizens elect
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Instead of a king, the people choose leaders to make decisions for them.
vocabulary.example: The founders wanted a government where voters choose their leaders, not one ruled by a king.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A republic is a country governed by elected representatives. The founders wanted the United States to be one.

vocabulary.definition: The branch or body of government that makes laws
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: The lawmakers. In the United States, it is Congress.
vocabulary.example: Congress, with its House and Senate, writes the nation's laws.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A legislature is a group of people who make laws. The national one is Congress.

vocabulary.definition: Having two houses, or parts, in a lawmaking body
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: From Latin words meaning "two rooms." Congress has two: the House and the Senate.
vocabulary.example: Under the Great Compromise, Congress was split into the House of Representatives and the Senate.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Bicameral means having two houses. Congress is made up of the House of Representatives and the Senate.

vocabulary.definition: The way people are given a voice in government through people who speak for them
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Having someone in government who speaks and votes for you.
vocabulary.example: Large states wanted seats in Congress to depend on population; small states wanted every state to count the same.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Representation is how people are given a voice in government. The delegates argued about how states should get seats in Congress.

vocabulary.definition: An agreement in which each side gives up part of what it wants
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: A deal where nobody gets everything, but everyone gets something.
vocabulary.example: Large states got seats based on population in the House, and small states got equal seats in the Senate.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A compromise is an agreement where each side gives up part of what it wants. The Constitution was built on several of them.

vocabulary.definition: The 1787 agreement that created a two-house Congress: the House based on population and the Senate with two members from every state
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: The deal that saved the convention by giving large states and small states each one house of Congress.
vocabulary.example: Roger Sherman of Connecticut suggested the plan, and it passed on July 16, 1787, by one vote.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: The Great Compromise created a Congress with two houses. Seats in the House depend on population, and every state has two senators.

vocabulary.definition: The 1787 agreement to count three out of every five enslaved people when dividing seats in the House
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: A counting rule that gave slaveholding states more power in Congress, even though enslaved people could not vote.
vocabulary.example: Because of this rule, southern states gained extra seats in the House until 1868.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: The Three-Fifths Compromise counted three out of every five enslaved people when dividing House seats. It gave slaveholding states more power.

vocabulary.definition: The plan written by James Madison that gave states seats in Congress based on population
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: The large states' plan: more people, more votes.
vocabulary.example: Edmund Randolph presented this plan on May 29, 1787, and it favored the states with the most people.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: The Virginia Plan gave each state seats in Congress based on its population. Large states supported it.

vocabulary.definition: The plan that kept a one-house Congress in which every state had one vote
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: The small states' plan: every state counts the same.
vocabulary.example: William Paterson offered this plan on June 15, 1787, to protect the small states.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: The New Jersey Plan gave every state one vote in a one-house Congress. Small states supported it.

vocabulary.definition: The introduction to the Constitution that explains its purpose
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: The opening sentence that says why the Constitution was written. It starts with "We the People."
vocabulary.example: The opening sentence lists six goals, from forming a more perfect union to protecting liberty for the future.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: The preamble is the introduction to the Constitution. It explains six goals of the new government.

vocabulary.definition: The idea that a government's power comes from the people
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: The people are the boss. The government only has power because the people agree to give it.
vocabulary.example: The words "We the People" show that the Constitution gets its power from citizens, not from the states or a king.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Popular sovereignty means the government's power comes from the people. The Constitution begins with "We the People."

vocabulary.definition: Dividing the work of government among three branches so no one group holds all the power
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Splitting the government's jobs into three parts so no single person can run everything.
vocabulary.example: Congress makes the laws, the president carries them out, and the courts decide what they mean.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Separation of powers divides the government into three branches. Each branch has its own job.

vocabulary.definition: The branch of government that makes laws, created by Article I
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: The lawmaking branch: Congress.
vocabulary.example: Article I describes this branch, which includes the House of Representatives and the Senate.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: The legislative branch makes the laws. It is Congress, created by Article I of the Constitution.

vocabulary.definition: The branch of government that carries out laws, led by the president and created by Article II
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: The branch that puts laws into action. The president is in charge of it.
vocabulary.example: Article II describes this branch, which commands the army and navy.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: The executive branch carries out the laws. It is led by the president and created by Article II.

vocabulary.definition: The branch of government that decides what laws mean, made up of the Supreme Court and other federal courts
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: The courts. They settle arguments about what the law says.
vocabulary.example: Article III creates the Supreme Court, and its judges serve for life.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: The judicial branch is the courts. It decides what laws mean and was created by Article III.

vocabulary.definition: The group of people chosen in each state who formally elect the president and vice president
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Voters choose electors, and electors choose the president. The word college here means a group, not a school.
vocabulary.example: Washington state casts 12 of these votes, and a candidate needs 270 of the 538 to win.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: The Electoral College is the group of electors who choose the president. A candidate needs 270 electoral votes to win.

vocabulary.definition: The system of dividing power between the national government and the state governments
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Two levels of government share power. The nation handles some jobs, and the states handle others.
vocabulary.example: The national government prints money, while states run schools and give driver's licenses.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Federalism divides power between the national government and the states. Some powers belong to each, and some are shared.

vocabulary.definition: Powers held by both the national government and the state governments
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Jobs both levels of government can do at the same time, like collecting taxes.
vocabulary.example: Both the national government and Washington state can collect taxes and build roads.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Concurrent powers belong to both the national and state governments. Both can collect taxes and set up courts.

vocabulary.definition: Powers kept by the states or the people because the Constitution does not give them to the national government
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Powers the states hold on to, like running schools.
vocabulary.example: Running public schools and setting driver's license rules are left to each state.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Reserved powers belong to the states. The Tenth Amendment says powers not given to the nation are kept by the states or the people.

vocabulary.definition: The system that gives each branch of government ways to limit the other two
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Each branch can stop the others from going too far.
vocabulary.example: A president can reject a bill, Congress can pass it anyway with a two-thirds vote, and the courts can strike it down.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Checks and balances give each branch ways to limit the others. This keeps any one branch from becoming too powerful.

vocabulary.definition: To reject a bill passed by Congress. Only a president can veto.
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: From a Latin word meaning "I forbid." Congress can override it with a two-thirds vote.
vocabulary.example: In 1792, George Washington sent a bill back to Congress unsigned for the first time.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: To veto a bill is to reject it. Only a president can veto, and Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in both houses.

vocabulary.definition: The process in which the House formally accuses an official of serious crimes, followed by a trial in the Senate
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: It is an accusation, not a removal. The Senate must hold a trial and vote to remove.
vocabulary.example: Andrew Johnson was formally accused by the House in 1868, and the Senate fell one vote short of removing him.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Impeachment is a formal accusation by the House. The Senate then holds a trial to decide whether to remove the official.

vocabulary.definition: The power of the courts to decide whether a law or government action follows the Constitution
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: The courts can cancel a law that breaks the Constitution.
vocabulary.example: In 1803, Chief Justice John Marshall ruled in Marbury v. Madison that part of a law could not stand.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Judicial review lets courts decide whether laws follow the Constitution. The Supreme Court first used it in 1803.

vocabulary.definition: The power of a nation or people to govern itself
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Being in charge of your own nation, with your own leaders, laws and courts.
vocabulary.example: Washington's 29 federally recognized tribes each have their own government, laws and courts.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Sovereignty is the power of a nation to govern itself. Tribal nations kept this power when the United States formed.

vocabulary.definition: A formal agreement between two or more nations
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: An official deal between nations. Under the Constitution, the president makes them and the Senate approves them.
vocabulary.example: In 1855, tribes around Puget Sound signed agreements with the United States that promised they could keep fishing.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A treaty is a formal agreement between nations. Two-thirds of the Senate must approve each one.

vocabulary.definition: The part of Article I that gives Congress power to regulate trade with foreign nations, among the states, and with tribes
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: The rule that puts Congress in charge of trade, and names tribes next to foreign nations and states.
vocabulary.example: Article I, Section 8, names "the Indian Tribes" in the same sentence as foreign nations and the states.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: The Commerce Clause gives Congress power over trade with other nations, between states and with tribes.

vocabulary.definition: The part of Article VI that makes the Constitution, national laws and treaties the supreme law of the land
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: When a state law conflicts with the Constitution, a national law or a treaty, the state law loses.
vocabulary.example: In 1974, a federal judge ruled that treaty fishing rights beat Washington's state fishing laws.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: The Supremacy Clause makes the Constitution, national laws and treaties the highest law. State laws cannot conflict with them.

vocabulary.definition: A time so long ago that no one can remember or measure it
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: A phrase many tribes use for how long their people have lived on their land: longer than anyone can count.
vocabulary.example: Washington's required tribal history curriculum is named for this phrase.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Time immemorial means a time so long ago that no one can remember or measure it.

vocabulary.definition: Land a tribe kept for itself in a treaty
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Tribes held on to this land when they gave up the rest. The United States did not give it to them.
vocabulary.example: The Nisqually kept a small part of their homeland in the 1854 Treaty of Medicine Creek.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A reservation is land a tribe kept in a treaty. The tribe held on to it while giving up other land.

vocabulary.definition: To formally give up land or power to another nation
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: To hand over land, usually in a treaty.
vocabulary.example: At Greenville in 1795, Native nations gave up most of present-day Ohio to the United States.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: To cede means to give up land. In the Treaty of Greenville, Native nations gave up most of Ohio.

vocabulary.definition: A line that marks the edge of a territory
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: A border line on a map.
vocabulary.example: The Greenville Treaty Line ran across Ohio from Lake Erie to the Ohio River.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A boundary is a line marking the edge of a territory. The Greenville Treaty drew one across Ohio.

vocabulary.definition: A formal promise
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: A promise written into an agreement.
vocabulary.example: The United States promised the nations they could live north of the Greenville line for as long as they wanted.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A guarantee is a formal promise. The Treaty of Greenville promised Native nations their land north of the line.

vocabulary.definition: To formally approve
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: To say an official yes. Nine states had to approve the Constitution before it took effect.
vocabulary.example: New Hampshire became the ninth state to approve the Constitution on June 21, 1788.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: To ratify means to formally approve. Nine states had to ratify the Constitution before it became law.

vocabulary.definition: A supporter of the Constitution and a stronger national government in 1787 and 1788
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Someone who said yes to the new Constitution.
vocabulary.example: Alexander Hamilton and James Madison argued for the new plan in newspaper essays.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A Federalist supported the Constitution. Federalists believed a stronger national government would fix the country's problems.

vocabulary.definition: An opponent of the Constitution in 1787 and 1788 who feared a strong national government and wanted a bill of rights
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Someone who said no to the Constitution without a list of rights.
vocabulary.example: George Mason and Patrick Henry worried that the new government could take away people's freedoms.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: An Anti-Federalist opposed the Constitution. They feared it gave the national government too much power.

vocabulary.definition: A series of 85 essays by Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay arguing for the Constitution
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Newspaper essays written under the made-up name Publius to convince New Yorkers to approve the Constitution.
vocabulary.example: Madison explained checks and balances in one of these essays in 1788.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: The Federalist Papers were 85 essays supporting the Constitution. Hamilton, Madison and Jay wrote them.

vocabulary.definition: A change or addition to the Constitution
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: A new rule added to the end of the Constitution. There are 27 of them.
vocabulary.example: The Nineteenth gave women the right to vote in 1920.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: An amendment is a change to the Constitution. It must be proposed and then ratified by three-fourths of the states.

vocabulary.definition: A formal suggestion for a change, the first step in amending the Constitution
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: A suggested change that still has to be approved.
vocabulary.example: Two-thirds of both the House and the Senate must vote yes before the states consider a change.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A proposal is a formal suggestion for a change. Two-thirds of Congress must vote for it.

vocabulary.definition: The first ten amendments to the Constitution, ratified in 1791
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: The list of rights the Anti-Federalists demanded, added to the Constitution in 1791.
vocabulary.example: James Madison proposed these amendments in 1789 to keep a promise made during ratification.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: The Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments to the Constitution. It protects freedoms such as speech and religion.

vocabulary.definition: Freedoms that belong to each person and that the government cannot take away
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Rights that belong to you as a person, like the right to speak your mind.
vocabulary.example: The First Amendment protects each person's religion, speech and press.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Individual rights belong to each person. The Bill of Rights protects many of them.

vocabulary.definition: The right to say what you think without being punished by the government
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: You can share your opinions, even unpopular ones. It has limits, like threats.
vocabulary.example: In 1969, the Supreme Court ruled that Mary Beth Tinker's black armband was protected.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Freedom of speech is the right to say what you think without government punishment. The First Amendment protects it.

vocabulary.definition: The rule that the government must follow fair procedures before it punishes anyone
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Before the government can punish you, it has to follow fair rules.
vocabulary.example: The Fifth Amendment says no one can lose life, liberty or property without fair legal steps.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Due process means the government must follow fair rules before punishing anyone. The Fifth Amendment requires it.

vocabulary.definition: A written order from a judge that allows police to search a place or arrest a person
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Permission from a judge that police usually need before searching a home.
vocabulary.example: Under the Fourth Amendment, police usually need a judge's permission to search a home.
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A warrant is a written order from a judge. Police usually need one to search a home.

timelineEvents.title: Articles of Confederation take effect
timelineEvents.description: Maryland becomes the thirteenth state to approve the Articles. The new national government has no president, no courts and no power to tax.

timelineEvents.title: Treaty of Paris ends the Revolutionary War
timelineEvents.description: Britain recognizes American independence and gives up its claim to land as far west as the Mississippi River.

timelineEvents.title: Shays' Rebellion begins
timelineEvents.description: Massachusetts farmers facing debt and lost farms close courts. Congress has no army to send.

timelineEvents.title: Constitutional Convention opens in Philadelphia
timelineEvents.description: Delegates from twelve states meet to fix the Articles and soon decide to write a new plan. George Washington presides.

timelineEvents.title: Northwest Ordinance passes
timelineEvents.description: Congress sets up a way for land north of the Ohio River to become new states and bans slavery there.

timelineEvents.title: Great Compromise passes by one vote
timelineEvents.description: Delegates agree to a two-house Congress: the House based on population and the Senate with two members per state.

timelineEvents.title: Delegates sign the Constitution
timelineEvents.description: Thirty-nine delegates sign. Now nine states must ratify it.

timelineEvents.title: The Federalist Papers begin
timelineEvents.description: Hamilton, Madison and Jay start publishing 85 essays in New York newspapers to argue for the Constitution.

timelineEvents.title: New Hampshire becomes the ninth state to ratify
timelineEvents.description: The Constitution takes effect. Virginia and New York ratify soon after, with promises of a bill of rights.

timelineEvents.title: George Washington becomes the first president
timelineEvents.description: Washington takes the oath of office in New York City, the first capital.

timelineEvents.title: Bill of Rights is ratified
timelineEvents.description: The first ten amendments become part of the Constitution, keeping the Federalists' promise.

timelineEvents.title: Battle of Fallen Timbers
timelineEvents.description: American troops defeat the Western Confederacy of Native nations near present-day Toledo, Ohio.

timelineEvents.title: Treaty of Greenville
timelineEvents.description: Native nations cede most of present-day Ohio. The United States promises the land north of the line is theirs.

timelineEvents.title: Marbury v. Madison
timelineEvents.description: The Supreme Court strikes down part of a law for the first time, establishing judicial review.

timelineEvents.title: Congress bans the Atlantic slave trade
timelineEvents.description: Congress passes the ban as soon as the Constitution allows; it takes effect on January 1, 1808.

timelineEvents.title: Treaty of Medicine Creek
timelineEvents.description: Nisqually, Puyallup and other tribes keep small reservations and the right to fish "at all usual and accustomed grounds."

timelineEvents.title: Thirteenth Amendment ends slavery
timelineEvents.description: After the Civil War, slavery is abolished, widening who counts as "We the People."

timelineEvents.title: Nineteenth Amendment ratified
timelineEvents.description: Women gain the right to vote after more than 70 years of organizing.

timelineEvents.title: Boldt decision
timelineEvents.description: A federal judge rules that Washington tribes' treaty fishing rights override state law.

practiceQuestions.question: Why did the first plan of government make the national government weak on purpose?
options: Americans feared a strong central power after fighting a king
The states wanted Britain to keep control of trade
Congress wanted the president to hold most of the power
The Native nations demanded a weak government
practiceQuestions.explanation: Americans had just fought a war against a king and Parliament, so they gave the new national government as little power as possible.

practiceQuestions.question: Which power did Congress NOT have under the Articles of Confederation?
options: Making treaties with other nations
Declaring war
Collecting taxes from the people
Running a post office
practiceQuestions.explanation: Congress could only ask the states for money. It had no power to tax, so it was always short of funds.

practiceQuestions.question: How many states had to agree before the Articles of Confederation could be changed?
options: Seven of the thirteen
Nine of the thirteen
Two-thirds of Congress
All thirteen
practiceQuestions.explanation: Every change needed all thirteen states, so one state could block any fix. Rhode Island's no vote stopped a national tax in 1782.

practiceQuestions.question: What was Shays' Rebellion?
options: A 1786 uprising of Massachusetts farmers facing debt and lost farms
A slave revolt in Virginia in 1787
A protest by small states at the convention
A British attack on the Northwest Territory
practiceQuestions.explanation: Farmers led by Daniel Shays, a war veteran, closed courts to stop judges from taking their farms for unpaid debts and taxes.

practiceQuestions.question: Why did Shays' Rebellion worry leaders like George Washington?
options: It proved the national government could not keep order
It showed that Britain was planning to return
It caused Congress to raise taxes too high
It made the states give up their militias
practiceQuestions.explanation: Congress had no army to send. Massachusetts had to pay for its own militia, which showed the national government was too weak to protect the country.

practiceQuestions.question: What did the Northwest Ordinance of 1787 do?
options: Set up a way for western land to become new states and banned slavery there
Gave the western land back to Britain
Created the Supreme Court
Allowed each state to print its own money
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Northwest Ordinance explained how territories north of the Ohio River could become states equal to the original thirteen, and it banned slavery there.

practiceQuestions.question: What was the original job of the delegates who met in Philadelphia in May 1787?
options: To fix, or revise, the Articles of Confederation
To declare independence from Britain
To elect the first president
To write a bill of rights
practiceQuestions.explanation: Congress called the meeting only to revise the Articles. The delegates decided instead to write an entirely new plan.

practiceQuestions.question: Which state refused to send delegates to Philadelphia in 1787?
options: Virginia
Rhode Island
New York
Pennsylvania
practiceQuestions.explanation: Rhode Island, which liked the weak system that let it act on its own, sent no one. Only twelve states took part.

practiceQuestions.question: Which group of people was included at the meeting in Philadelphia?
options: Women who owned property
Enslaved people
Leaders of Native nations
White men, many of them wealthy
practiceQuestions.explanation: All 55 delegates were white men, and most were wealthy. Women, enslaved people, free Black Americans and Native nations had no one there.

practiceQuestions.question: Why did the delegates keep their meetings secret?
options: So they could change their minds and argue freely
Because Britain had spies in Philadelphia
Because Congress had banned the meeting
So the newspapers would not report on Washington
practiceQuestions.explanation: With the windows shut and guards at the door, delegates could change positions without public pressure. Most of what we know comes from James Madison's notes.

practiceQuestions.question: Who was chosen to lead the meeting in Philadelphia?
options: Benjamin Franklin
James Madison
George Washington
Alexander Hamilton
practiceQuestions.explanation: The delegates elected George Washington to preside. His reputation gave the meeting trust.

practiceQuestions.question: What did the Virginia Plan propose?
options: Every state gets one vote in Congress
States with more people get more seats in Congress
The president chooses members of Congress
Congress is removed and replaced by a king
practiceQuestions.explanation: James Madison's plan tied representation to population, which favored large states like Virginia.

practiceQuestions.question: Why did small states like New Jersey and Delaware oppose the Virginia Plan?
options: They feared large states would outvote them
They wanted a king instead of Congress
They had more people than the large states
They wanted to end the Union
practiceQuestions.explanation: If seats depended on population, big states would control every vote. Small states wanted each state to count equally.

practiceQuestions.question: How did the Great Compromise settle the fight between large and small states?
options: It created one house based on population and one house with equal votes per state
It gave every state the same number of seats in both houses
It let the president decide how many seats each state gets
It ended Congress and gave all power to the states
practiceQuestions.explanation: The House of Representatives is based on population; the Senate gives every state two senators. Congress became bicameral.

practiceQuestions.question: Who proposed the Great Compromise?
options: George Washington
Roger Sherman of Connecticut
Patrick Henry
John Jay
practiceQuestions.explanation: Roger Sherman, from a middle-sized state, suggested a plan with something for both sides. It passed by one vote on July 16, 1787.

practiceQuestions.question: What does bicameral mean?
options: Having two houses in a lawmaking body
Having two presidents
Having two capitals
Having two constitutions
practiceQuestions.explanation: Bicameral comes from Latin words for "two rooms." Congress has the House and the Senate.

practiceQuestions.question: Why did southern delegates want enslaved people counted when dividing seats in the House?
options: To give their states more seats and more power
Because enslaved people would be allowed to vote
To lower their taxes to zero
To free enslaved people sooner
practiceQuestions.explanation: Counting enslaved people raised the South's population and its seats, even though enslaved people had no vote and no rights.

practiceQuestions.question: Under the Three-Fifths Compromise, how were enslaved people counted?
options: Each enslaved person counted as one full person
Three out of every five enslaved people were counted
Enslaved people were not counted at all
Five out of every three were counted
practiceQuestions.explanation: Three out of every five enslaved people were added to a state's population for House seats and for direct taxes.

practiceQuestions.question: What did delegates agree about the Atlantic slave trade?
options: Congress could not ban it before 1808
It was banned immediately
Each state had to ban it by 1790
It was left out of the Constitution forever
practiceQuestions.explanation: To keep Georgia and South Carolina in the union, the delegates agreed that Congress could not end the trade before 1808. Congress banned it that year.

practiceQuestions.question: What did the Fugitive Slave Clause require?
options: People who escaped slavery had to be returned, even from free states
Free states had to ban slavery
Enslaved people could buy their freedom
Congress had to pay slaveholders for escaped people
practiceQuestions.explanation: The clause required free states to return people who had escaped slavery, which tied the whole nation to protecting slavery.

practiceQuestions.question: Which statement about the Constitution and slavery is accurate?
options: It protected slavery without ever using the word "slave"
It banned slavery in all thirteen states
It said nothing that affected slavery
It gave enslaved people the right to vote
practiceQuestions.explanation: The delegates used phrases like "other persons" and "person held to service" so the word never appears, yet several clauses protected slavery.

practiceQuestions.question: Why do historians say the compromises over slavery came at a cost?
options: They kept the union together while leaving millions of people enslaved
They made the Constitution too long to read
They gave Britain power over the South
They forced northern states to adopt slavery
practiceQuestions.explanation: The compromises got all the states to sign, but they protected slavery and pushed the conflict to a later generation.

practiceQuestions.question: What do the words "We the People" at the start of the Constitution show?
options: The government's power comes from the people
The states are more powerful than the nation
The president holds all power
Only property owners could read it
practiceQuestions.explanation: This is popular sovereignty. The Articles began with the states; the Constitution begins with the people.

practiceQuestions.question: Which of these is one of the goals listed in the preamble?
options: To form a more perfect union
To create a national religion
To guarantee every citizen a job
To expand west to the Pacific
practiceQuestions.explanation: The preamble lists six goals, including to form a more perfect union, establish justice and secure the blessings of liberty.

practiceQuestions.question: Which branch of government makes laws?
options: The executive branch
The judicial branch
The legislative branch
The state branch
practiceQuestions.explanation: The legislative branch, Congress, is described in Article I and makes the laws.

practiceQuestions.question: Which article of the Constitution describes the president and the executive branch?
options: Article I
Article II
Article III
Article VII
practiceQuestions.explanation: Article I covers Congress, Article II the president, and Article III the courts.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the job of the judicial branch?
options: To decide what laws mean and settle disputes
To make new laws
To command the army
To collect taxes
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Supreme Court and other federal courts interpret laws and decide cases.

practiceQuestions.question: Why did the framers divide the government into three branches?
options: So no single person or group could hold all the power
Because there were three large states
So each branch could make its own laws
Because Britain had three branches
practiceQuestions.explanation: This is separation of powers. The framers believed concentrated power leads to tyranny.

practiceQuestions.question: The president vetoes a bill. What can Congress do?
options: Nothing; the bill is dead forever
Override the veto with a two-thirds vote in both houses
Ask the Supreme Court to sign it
Pass it with a simple majority in the House only
practiceQuestions.explanation: An override needs two-thirds of both the House and the Senate. This is a check on the president.

practiceQuestions.question: Which is an example of the judicial branch checking Congress?
options: Ruling that a law goes against the Constitution
Vetoing a bill
Approving a treaty
Declaring war
practiceQuestions.explanation: Judicial review lets courts strike down laws that break the Constitution. The Supreme Court first used it in Marbury v. Madison in 1803.

practiceQuestions.question: Which is a check that Congress has on the president?
options: Approving or rejecting the president's choices for judges
Choosing the president's cabinet without asking
Serving as commander in chief
Interpreting the Constitution
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Senate must approve the president's nominations for judges and other top jobs, and Congress can impeach and remove a president.

practiceQuestions.question: What does impeachment mean?
options: The House formally accuses an official of serious wrongdoing
The president is automatically removed from office
The Supreme Court cancels an election
A state leaves the union
practiceQuestions.explanation: Impeachment is an accusation. The Senate then holds a trial, and two-thirds must vote to remove the official.

practiceQuestions.question: How is the president chosen?
options: Voters choose electors, and the Electoral College elects the president
Congress votes for the president
The Supreme Court picks the president
Governors of each state choose the president
practiceQuestions.explanation: Voters in each state pick electors. A candidate needs 270 of the 538 electoral votes to win.

practiceQuestions.question: Why does a state like California have more electoral votes than Washington?
options: Electoral votes equal a state's seats in the House plus its two senators
California joined the union earlier
Every state gets the same number of electoral votes
California pays more taxes
practiceQuestions.explanation: Each state's electoral votes equal its House seats plus two senators. More people means more House seats.

practiceQuestions.question: What is federalism?
options: Dividing power between the national government and the states
Giving all power to the national government
Letting each city write its own constitution
Combining the three branches into one
practiceQuestions.explanation: Under federalism, some powers belong to the nation, some to the states, and some are shared.

practiceQuestions.question: Which power belongs only to the national government?
options: Printing money
Running public schools
Issuing driver's licenses
Holding state elections
practiceQuestions.explanation: Printing money, declaring war and making treaties are national powers. Schools and licenses are reserved to the states.

practiceQuestions.question: Collecting taxes and building roads are examples of what kind of powers?
options: Concurrent powers
Reserved powers
Veto powers
Judicial powers
practiceQuestions.explanation: Concurrent powers are shared by the national and state governments.

practiceQuestions.question: What does the Supremacy Clause say?
options: The Constitution, national laws and treaties are the highest law of the land
The president is above the law
State laws override national laws
The Supreme Court can write new laws
practiceQuestions.explanation: Article VI makes the Constitution, federal laws and treaties supreme. A state law that conflicts with them cannot stand.

practiceQuestions.question: Why did the framers make the Constitution possible to amend, but hard to amend?
options: So it could change over time, but not on a whim
So only the president could change it
So it would never need to change
So each state could change it alone
practiceQuestions.explanation: An amendment needs two-thirds of Congress to propose it and three-fourths of the states to ratify it. Only 27 have passed.

practiceQuestions.question: How did the Constitution treat Native nations?
options: As separate nations that the United States dealt with by treaty
As part of the states they lived near
As citizens of the United States
It did not mention them at all
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Commerce Clause names "the Indian Tribes" alongside foreign nations and states, and the government made treaties with them.

practiceQuestions.question: What does the Commerce Clause give Congress power over?
options: Trade with foreign nations, among the states, and with tribes
All schools in the country
The choice of state governors
The size of the Supreme Court
practiceQuestions.explanation: Article I, Section 8 lists these three kinds of trade. Naming tribes there treated them as nations.

practiceQuestions.question: Who must approve a treaty before it takes effect?
options: Two-thirds of the Senate
A majority of the House
The Supreme Court
Three-fourths of the states
practiceQuestions.explanation: The president makes treaties, but two-thirds of the Senate must approve them.

practiceQuestions.question: What happened at the Battle of Fallen Timbers in 1794?
options: American troops defeated a confederacy of Native nations in Ohio
Britain won back the Northwest Territory
Native nations captured Philadelphia
The Constitution was signed
practiceQuestions.explanation: General Anthony Wayne's army defeated the Western Confederacy, which led to the Treaty of Greenville the next year.

practiceQuestions.question: What did Native nations give up in the Treaty of Greenville (1795)?
options: Most of present-day Ohio
All land east of the Mississippi River
Their right to govern themselves
Nothing; they gained land
practiceQuestions.explanation: The nations ceded most of Ohio south of the Greenville line, while the United States promised the land north of the line was theirs.

practiceQuestions.question: Why can tribes in Washington state fish in places where state rules might not allow it?
options: Treaties promised those rights, and treaties are the supreme law of the land
Washington never made fishing laws
Tribes bought the rivers from the state
The president gave special permission each year
practiceQuestions.explanation: The 1850s treaties reserved fishing rights. In 1974 a federal judge ruled that, under the Supremacy Clause, the treaties override state law.

practiceQuestions.question: What does sovereignty mean for a tribal nation today?
options: The tribe governs itself with its own leaders, laws and courts
The tribe must follow only state laws
The tribe belongs to the nearest city
The tribe has no government
practiceQuestions.explanation: Washington has 29 federally recognized tribes. Each is a sovereign nation that governs itself.

practiceQuestions.question: What is a reservation?
options: Land a tribe kept for itself in a treaty
Land the government gave to tribes as a gift
A national park
A city founded by settlers
practiceQuestions.explanation: Tribes reserved, or kept, that land when they gave up other land. The United States did not give it to them.

practiceQuestions.question: Which statement about treaties between the United States and Native nations is accurate?
options: The United States often broke the promises made in them
They were always kept exactly as written
They were never approved by the Senate
They gave Native nations the right to vote in Congress
practiceQuestions.explanation: Settlers and the government repeatedly broke treaty promises, but tribes have used the treaties in court to defend their rights.

practiceQuestions.question: How many states had to ratify the Constitution for it to take effect?
options: All thirteen
Nine
Seven
Eleven
practiceQuestions.explanation: Nine states were needed. New Hampshire became the ninth on June 21, 1788.

practiceQuestions.question: What did Federalists believe?
options: A stronger national government would fix the country's problems
The Articles of Confederation worked well
The states should leave the union
The country needed a king
practiceQuestions.explanation: Federalists like Hamilton and Madison argued that the Articles had failed and the Constitution would bring order.

practiceQuestions.question: What was the main thing Anti-Federalists wanted added to the Constitution?
options: A bill of rights
A king
A state religion
More power for the president
practiceQuestions.explanation: Anti-Federalists feared a strong government could take away freedoms unless rights were written down.

practiceQuestions.question: What were The Federalist Papers?
options: 85 newspaper essays arguing for the Constitution
The minutes of the Philadelphia meeting
Letters from Anti-Federalists to the king
The first ten amendments
practiceQuestions.explanation: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay wrote them under the name Publius to persuade New Yorkers.

practiceQuestions.question: How did Federalists win ratification in states like Massachusetts and Virginia?
options: They promised to add a bill of rights after ratification
They threatened to bring back the king
They paid each delegate
They let those states write their own constitutions
practiceQuestions.explanation: The promise of amendments won over enough doubters. Madison kept it by proposing amendments in 1789.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the Bill of Rights?
options: The first ten amendments to the Constitution
The Declaration of Independence
The list of the president's powers
A law passed by the first Congress
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Bill of Rights was ratified in 1791 and protects freedoms such as speech, religion and a fair trial.

practiceQuestions.question: Which freedoms does the First Amendment protect?
options: Religion, speech, press, assembly and petition
The right to bear arms
Protection from unreasonable searches
The right to a jury trial
practiceQuestions.explanation: The First Amendment protects five freedoms. The others listed are in the Second, Fourth and Sixth Amendments.

practiceQuestions.question: What does the Fourth Amendment protect against?
options: Unreasonable searches and seizures
Cruel and unusual punishment
Being forced to house soldiers
Losing the right to vote
practiceQuestions.explanation: Police usually need a warrant, signed by a judge, before searching a home.

practiceQuestions.question: What does due process mean?
options: The government must follow fair procedures before punishing anyone
Police can arrest anyone at any time
The president decides who goes to jail
Courts must finish every case in a week
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Fifth Amendment says no person can lose life, liberty or property without due process of law.

practiceQuestions.question: What does the Tenth Amendment say?
options: Powers not given to the national government belong to the states or the people
The president can serve only two terms
Women have the right to vote
Slavery is banned
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Tenth Amendment protects reserved powers, a key part of federalism.

practiceQuestions.question: In Tinker v. Des Moines (1969), what did the Supreme Court decide?
options: Students keep their right to free speech at school
Schools can ban any student opinion
Students have no rights until age 18
Only teachers have free speech at school
practiceQuestions.explanation: The court ruled that students wearing black armbands to protest a war were protected, as long as they did not seriously disrupt school.

practiceQuestions.question: Which amendment ended slavery?
options: The Thirteenth Amendment
The First Amendment
The Tenth Amendment
The Nineteenth Amendment
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Thirteenth Amendment, ratified in 1865, abolished slavery. Later amendments widened who counted as "the People."

practiceQuestions.question: Which amendment gave women the right to vote?
options: The Fifteenth Amendment
The Nineteenth Amendment
The Twenty-Sixth Amendment
The Fourteenth Amendment
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Nineteenth Amendment was ratified in 1920 after decades of work by activists such as Alice Paul.

shortAnswerQuestions.question: Why did the Articles of Confederation fail? Explain two weaknesses and what happened because of them.
shortAnswerQuestions.rubric: Strong response names two specific weaknesses (no power to tax, no army, every change needed all thirteen states, no president or courts) and connects each to a real result, such as unpaid debts or Shays' Rebellion.
shortAnswerQuestions.exemplar: The Articles of Confederation failed because the national government was too weak to solve the country's problems. First, Congress had no power to tax, so it could only ask the states for money. When the states did not pay, Congress could not pay its war debts or its soldiers. Second, Congress had no army. When farmers in Massachusetts rebelled in 1786, Congress could not stop them, so Massachusetts had to raise its own militia. Shays' Rebellion showed leaders like George Washington that the country needed a stronger government.

plan.text: The Articles of Confederation failed because the national government was too weak to solve the country's problems.
Congress had no power to tax, so it could not pay its war debts or soldiers.
Congress had no army, so it could not stop Shays' Rebellion in 1786.
These failures convinced leaders that the country needed a stronger government, which led to the meeting in Philadelphia.

sentenceStarters: The Articles of Confederation failed because ___.
One weakness was ___, which led to ___.

shortAnswerQuestions.question: Was the Great Compromise fair to both large and small states? Explain what each side gained and gave up.
shortAnswerQuestions.rubric: Strong response takes a clear position, explains what large states wanted (Virginia Plan) and what small states wanted (New Jersey Plan), and shows how the two houses gave each side part of what it wanted.
shortAnswerQuestions.exemplar: The Great Compromise was fair because each side got something important. Large states like Virginia wanted seats based on population, so they would have more votes. Small states like New Jersey wanted every state to have an equal vote. The compromise created a bicameral Congress. In the House of Representatives, states with more people get more seats. In the Senate, every state gets two senators. Large states gave up full control, and small states gave up equal votes in both houses, but each side got one house that protected it.

plan.text: The Great Compromise was fair because each side got one house that protected it.
Large states got the House of Representatives, where seats depend on population.
Small states got the Senate, where every state has two senators.
Neither side got everything, but each side gave up part of what it wanted so the union could stay together.

sentenceStarters: The Great Compromise was (fair / not fair) because ___.
Large states wanted ___, while small states wanted ___.
In the end, each side gave up ___.

shortAnswerQuestions.question: The Constitution never uses the word "slave," yet it protected slavery. Explain how, and what the compromises over slavery cost.
shortAnswerQuestions.rubric: Strong response explains at least two clauses (Three-Fifths, slave trade until 1808, Fugitive Slave Clause), explains why the delegates agreed to them, and evaluates who paid the cost.
shortAnswerQuestions.exemplar: The Constitution protected slavery in several ways without ever saying the word. The Three-Fifths Compromise counted three out of every five enslaved people when dividing seats in the House, which gave slaveholding states more power even though enslaved people could not vote. The Constitution also stopped Congress from banning the slave trade before 1808 and required people who escaped slavery to be returned. Delegates agreed to these deals to keep the southern states in the union. The cost was paid by enslaved people, who were excluded from "We the People" and stayed enslaved for decades.

plan.text: The Constitution protected slavery through several compromises, and enslaved people paid the cost.
The Three-Fifths Compromise gave slaveholding states extra seats in the House.
Congress could not ban the slave trade before 1808, and people who escaped had to be returned.
Delegates made these deals to keep the South in the union, but they left millions of people enslaved.

sentenceStarters: The people who paid the cost were ___ because ___.

shortAnswerQuestions.question: How do checks and balances keep any one branch from becoming too powerful? Give two real examples.
shortAnswerQuestions.rubric: Strong response explains separation of powers, gives two specific checks between different branches (veto, override, judicial review, impeachment, Senate approval), and explains how each one limits power.
shortAnswerQuestions.exemplar: Checks and balances give each branch ways to limit the other two, so no branch can take over. For example, the president can veto a bill that Congress passes, but Congress can override the veto with a two-thirds vote in both houses. The courts can also check both branches with judicial review: in Marbury v. Madison in 1803, the Supreme Court ruled that part of a law broke the Constitution. Because each branch can block the others, power stays divided, which is what the framers wanted after living under a king.

plan.text: Checks and balances keep any one branch from taking over by letting each branch limit the others.
The president can veto a bill, but Congress can override it with a two-thirds vote.
The courts can strike down a law that breaks the Constitution, as in Marbury v. Madison.
Because every branch can be blocked, power stays divided, which protects people from tyranny.

shortAnswerQuestions.question: Why are treaties with Native nations still important in Washington state today? Use the Constitution in your answer.
shortAnswerQuestions.rubric: Strong response explains that the Constitution treats tribes as nations (Commerce Clause, treaties), that the Supremacy Clause makes treaties the supreme law, and connects this to a real example such as treaty fishing rights and the 1974 Boldt decision.
shortAnswerQuestions.exemplar: Treaties with Native nations are still important because the Constitution makes them part of the supreme law of the land. The Commerce Clause names tribes alongside foreign nations, which shows that the United States treated them as sovereign nations. In the 1850s, tribes around Puget Sound signed treaties that promised they could keep fishing in their usual places. When Washington tried to limit that fishing, a federal judge ruled in 1974 that the treaties override state law because of the Supremacy Clause. Today, Washington's 29 tribes still use those treaties to protect their rights.

plan.text: Treaties with Native nations still matter because the Constitution makes them the supreme law of the land.
The Commerce Clause names tribes alongside foreign nations and states.
In 1974, a federal judge ruled that treaty fishing rights beat Washington's state fishing laws.
Because treaties are supreme, tribes can use them in court to protect their sovereignty and rights today.

sentenceStarters: Treaties with Native nations still matter because ___.

shortAnswerQuestions.question: Which right in the Bill of Rights matters most to you, and why did the Anti-Federalists think it needed to be written down?
shortAnswerQuestions.rubric: Strong response names a specific right and amendment, explains why it matters with a realistic example, and connects to the Anti-Federalist fear that a strong national government could take away freedoms.
shortAnswerQuestions.exemplar: The right that matters most to me is freedom of speech, which the First Amendment protects. It lets me share my opinions, even if the government or other people disagree. In 1969, the Supreme Court ruled in Tinker v. Des Moines that students keep this right at school. The Anti-Federalists wanted rights like this written down because they had just fought a king who punished people for speaking out. They feared a strong national government could do the same, so they refused to support the Constitution until Federalists promised to add a bill of rights.

plan.text: The right that matters most to me is ___, protected by the ___ Amendment.
This right lets people ___. For example, ___.
Anti-Federalists refused to support the Constitution until a bill of rights was promised.
They feared a strong government could take away freedoms, just as the king had.

sentenceStarters: The right that matters most to me is ___ because ___.
The Anti-Federalists wanted it written down because ___.

typingPassages.title: A Government Too Weak to Work
typingPassages.source: Written for the Building a Government unit
typingPassages.passage: After the Revolution, Americans feared a powerful central government, so the Articles of Confederation kept the states strong and Congress weak. Congress could not collect taxes, raise an army or settle fights between states, and every change needed all thirteen states to agree. When Massachusetts farmers rose up in Shays' Rebellion in 1786, Congress had no way to stop them. Leaders like George Washington decided the country needed a stronger plan, and in May 1787 delegates met in Philadelphia.

typingPassages.title: Two Houses and a Hard Bargain
typingPassages.source: Written for the Building a Government unit
typingPassages.passage: The biggest fight in Philadelphia was over representation. Large states wanted seats based on population, and small states wanted every state to count the same. Roger Sherman of Connecticut offered the Great Compromise: a bicameral Congress with a House based on population and a Senate with two members from every state. The delegates also argued over slavery. Under the Three-Fifths Compromise, three out of every five enslaved people were counted for House seats, giving slaveholding states more power.

typingPassages.title: Power Divided Three Ways
typingPassages.source: Written for the Building a Government unit
typingPassages.passage: The Constitution begins with "We the People," showing that the government's power comes from the people. To keep any one group from taking over, the framers used separation of powers. The legislative branch makes laws, the executive branch carries them out, and the judicial branch decides what they mean. Through checks and balances, each branch can limit the others. Federalism divides power again, this time between the national government and the states.

typingPassages.title: Nations Within a Nation
typingPassages.source: Written for the Building a Government unit
typingPassages.passage: The Constitution treated Native nations as separate nations. The Commerce Clause gave Congress power over trade with tribes, and the United States made treaties with them. The Supremacy Clause made every treaty part of the supreme law of the land. The government often broke those promises, but treaties still matter. In 1974, a federal judge ruled that treaty fishing rights in Washington override state law, and the state's 29 tribes govern themselves today.

typingPassages.title: A Promise Kept
typingPassages.source: Written for the Building a Government unit
typingPassages.passage: Before the Constitution could take effect, nine states had to ratify it. Federalists argued that a stronger government would fix the country's problems. Anti-Federalists feared it would take away freedoms and demanded a bill of rights. To win ratification, Federalists promised to add one. James Madison kept that promise, and in 1791 the first ten amendments became the Bill of Rights, protecting freedom of speech, religion and the press, along with the right to due process.

quotes.text: We the People of the United States, in Order to form a more perfect Union...
quotes.author: The Preamble
quotes.source: The Constitution of the United States, 1787

quotes.text: If men were angels, no government would be necessary.
quotes.author: James Madison

quotes.text: Ambition must be made to counteract ambition.
quotes.author: James Madison

quotes.text: I confess that there are several parts of this constitution which I do not at present approve, but I am not sure I shall never approve them.
quotes.author: Benjamin Franklin
quotes.source: Speech at the Constitutional Convention, September 17, 1787, from James Madison’s notes

quotes.text: A bill of rights is what the people are entitled to against every government on earth.
quotes.author: Thomas Jefferson

funFacts.text: Jacob Shallus, a clerk for the Pennsylvania legislature, handwrote the final copy of the Constitution and was paid $30 for the job.
The delegates promised to keep their debates secret. James Madison's notes were not published until 1840, four years after he died.
At 81, Benjamin Franklin was the oldest delegate. The youngest, Jonathan Dayton of New Jersey, was 26.
Congress sent 12 amendments to the states in 1789, and 10 were ratified in 1791. One of the other two finally became the 27th Amendment in 1992.
Rhode Island was the last of the thirteen states to ratify, in May 1790, more than a year after Washington became president.
The word "slave" does not appear anywhere in the original Constitution. It first appears in the Thirteenth Amendment, which ended slavery in 1865.

powerSorts.title: Which Branch?
powerSorts.prompt: Which branch of the national government has this power?

items.explanation: Article I gives Congress the power to make laws.
Only Congress can declare war, even though the president commands the military.

items.text: Decides how to spend the nation's money
items.explanation: Congress controls the budget. Spending bills start in the House.

items.text: Overrides a veto with a two-thirds vote
items.explanation: If two-thirds of both the House and the Senate vote again, a bill becomes law without the president.

items.text: Approves treaties with a two-thirds vote
items.explanation: The president makes treaties, but two-thirds of the Senate must approve them.
The House impeaches, or accuses, and the Senate holds the trial. Both are part of Congress.

items.text: Approves the president's choices for judges
items.explanation: The Senate must confirm judges and other top officials, a check on the president.

items.text: Carries out and enforces the laws
items.explanation: Article II puts the president in charge of carrying out the laws Congress passes.
The president is commander in chief, so the military answers to an elected civilian.
A veto is the president's check on Congress.
The president makes treaties. The Senate then approves or rejects them.
The president nominates justices, and the Senate confirms them.

items.text: Pardons people convicted of federal crimes
items.explanation: Article II gives the president the power to pardon.

items.text: Decides whether a law follows the Constitution
items.explanation: This is judicial review, first used in Marbury v. Madison in 1803.

items.text: Decides what a law means in a real case
items.explanation: Courts apply and interpret laws when people disagree about them.
Article III gives federal courts the power to hear cases between states.

items.text: Can declare an action of the president unconstitutional
items.explanation: The courts check the president as well as Congress.

powerSorts.title: National, State or Both?
powerSorts.prompt: Under federalism, who holds this power?

items.explanation: One national money lets people trade across state lines. Under the Articles, states printed their own.
Only the national government can declare war, so the country speaks with one voice.
The Constitution bars states from making treaties.
Article I gives Congress the power to set up post offices.
The Commerce Clause gives this power to Congress.
Defense is a national job. Congress raises and pays for the military.

items.text: Deals with tribal nations through treaties and trade
items.explanation: The Commerce Clause and the treaty power put relations with tribes in national hands.
Education is a reserved power. States and local school districts run schools.
Each state sets its own rules for licenses.

items.text: Sets up city and county governments
items.explanation: Local governments are created by the states.
Marriage licenses come from the state, usually through a county office.
States run elections, even for national offices, though the Constitution and Congress set some rules.
Taxing is a concurrent power. You may pay both federal and state taxes.
Both levels pay for roads. Interstate highways use national and state money.
There are federal courts and state courts.
Both the national government and the states can borrow money.
Congress and every state legislature make laws. Police enforce both.
